About me

I love  building things and solving problems.

This is my story, along with some flicks from my travels

Scroll Down

The Past: Curiosity, Frustration, and Stubborn Persistence

I’ve been curious about how things work for as long as I can remember. As a kid, that curiosity usually looked like unscrewing remote controls, tinkering with old laptops, and breaking computers just to see if I could fix them again. Computers felt like magic, but the kind of magic that rewarded patience and persistence.

Around the age of 12, I picked up a dusty Python book and started teaching myself how to code. I’d played with Scratch before, but Python felt different. Real. Powerful. I started small: tiny programs to automate parts of my life, simple games, and even a website that (questionably) unblocked games on school computers. Most of what I built barely worked at first, but the feeling of finally seeing something run kept me going.

That persistence wasn’t limited to code. I was never “naturally good” at math. In fact, I failed my first math exam in high school. But instead of accepting that as a limitation, I doubled down. I practiced relentlessly, asked questions, and refused to give up. That mindset paid off: by the end of high school, I achieved the highest mark in the world in not only A-Level Mathematics, but also Physics.

That experience shaped how I approach everything I do. I learned that talent matters far less than effort, consistency, and a willingness to sit with frustration. Whether I’m debugging code or learning something entirely new, I believe in putting in the work and taking pride in the craft.

The Present: Learning Across Borders and Disciplines

Today, I’m a Computer Science junior at NYU Abu Dhabi, with minors in Economics and Applied Mathematics. Over the past three years, my education has taken me to more than 30 cities across the world. Each one left a quiet but lasting mark on how I think.

I’ve studied business and technology in New York, struggled my way through learning French in Paris, learned from inspiring young entrepreneurs in Kigali, explored Mediterranean foodways across Italy, and even tried building a startup in San Francisco. Each place taught me something different about people, systems, and the problems worth solving.

Academically, I’m deeply interested in AI and machine learning. I currently work as a research assistant focusing on large language models, particularly protein LLMs for drug discovery, and on fine-tuning models for real-world industrial and biological applications. Alongside research, I love building clean, pixel-perfect interfaces and thinking deeply about human-computer interaction: how technology feels, not just how it functions.

Outside of work, you’ll probably find me playing badminton, backpacking through a new city with nothing but a camera and some friends, discovering new foods, or reading fiction. I’m also trying (and mostly succeeding) to maintain a 500+ day Duolingo streak in French.

The Future: Open Questions, Grounded Principles

I don’t have a rigid 10-year plan, and I’m okay with that. What I do have are principles I trust: curiosity, discipline, and a belief that technology should serve people, not the other way around.

Maybe I’ll join industry and build meaningful software. Maybe I’ll continue my LLM research into graduate school. Maybe I’ll found a startup. What I know for sure is that I want to use my skills to help others and keep adding countries to a very long bucket list along the way.

Whatever the future holds, I’ll keep chasing that familiar rush: the moment when something finally works. The quiet pride of learning something new. The satisfaction of leaving a system just a little better than I found it.

The future’s a blank canvas, and I’ve still got a lot of paint left.

Thanks for stopping by!
